claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy with a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial catalyst has low platinum-group-metal content.
A single-stage, controlled low-temperature oxidative heat treatment will induce surface segregation.
The oxidative heat treatment will form nanoscale Pt-Cu-enriched clusters or a core-shell structure at the catalyst surface.
The surface segregation will preserve the integrity of the underlying multi-principal-element alloy.
The oxidative pretreatment causes controlled redistribution of Pt and Cu toward the surface.
Segregated Pt-Cu surface regions enhance oxidation kinetics.
Enhanced oxidation kinetics will lower the light-off temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation relative to the untreated catalyst.
Pt is resistant to poisoning by H2O and NO.
The Pt-Cu-enriched surface will produce a smaller activity loss in the presence of H2O and NO than the untreated catalyst.
The treatment-induced nanostructure will mitigate catalytic degradation during long-term operation.
The treated catalyst will retain more oxidation activity over accelerated aging cycles than the untreated catalyst.
The predicted benefits apply under transient exhaust operation below 150 °C with realistic H2O and NO levels.
Accelerated aging cycles can be configured to simulate full vehicle-lifetime mileage degradation.
